title: Three Positive Things About Yesterday's Gyrations in the Stock Market
text:
Three Positive Things About Yesterday's Gyrations in the Stock Market October 24, 2018, 09:59:16
Looked at logically, every downturn in the stock market such as we have experienced over the last three weeks is essentially a triumph of fear over experience. There have been many such selloffs over the years, with at least a dozen since the recession technically ended in 2009 alone.
While it may seem obvious, it is worth pointing out that so far, none of them have been terminal. The market has always bounced back, and as long as the capitalist system survives, always will.
Still, with stocks bouncing around but sharply lower, most investors are probably nervous and desperately looking for some good news. Fortunately, yesterday provided a few reasons to be cheerful.
The first was the day’s price action, and the reasons behind it. The morning started by generating the kind of sick-to-the-stomach feeling that has become all too familiar recently, with the Dow opening over 250 points lower than Monday’s close and quickly heading south.
As the day wore on though, buyers began to poke their heads above the parapets. By the time all was said and done, the index closed “only” 125 points down.
That may seem like a Pyrrhic victory, but the encouraging part comes from what caused the intraday turnaround: nothing.
The lower opening was the result of a couple of high-profile earnings disappointments, but there was no specific good news that turned sentiment around.
If we extend the chart out it starts to look like proximity to the end of 2017 level was a wake-up call, prompting traders to see value at these levels. That is encouraging because it shows that, absent any scary news, there are still buyers around.
The second reason for optimism is a bit more obscure and wonkish but will probably turn out to be more important in the long run.
As this insightful WSJ article by Amrith Rankumar points out, one of the most notable things for many analysts about this market move is that stocks, commodities, and even at times bonds, have been moving together much of the time. That indicates a move driven by naked fear rather than rational analysis.
That may not seem like a good thing, but it is. Fear fades, facts don’t. It is hard, maybe even impossible to predict when a fear-driven move will turn around, but it certainly will at some point, and when it does the bounce back tends to be quite rapid as well.
The third thing that investors can draw encouragement from in yesterday’s market is the performance of some individual stocks. Large tech companies such as Apple ( AAPL ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ) had positive days. That hints at a breakdown in the kind of correlation mentioned in Rankumar’s piece, at least when it comes to stocks.
To put it another way, rational decisions are being made. As I said above, predicting the end of fear is hard, but it is far more likely once rationality returns in at least some form.
I am not yet ready to say that this period of volatility is over. The fears are not completely irrational. They are grounded in specific things such as the effects of tariffs, higher interest rates, and large and growing debt in the U.S. and any suggestion that those fears are justified would kick things off again. It is therefore too early to say that yesterday’s market marked the end of this retracement, but there were, finally, some positive signs.
